choices.why: The juxtaposition 'ὁ μὲν Υἱός, τὰ δὲ, δοῦλα' sets up a stark contrast: the Son versus the created order, which is portrayed as servile.
The phrase 'ἐν δεξιᾷ' is a fixed biblical idiom denoting honor and shared rule, not merely spatial location.
The comparative 'κρείττων' is used substantively to refer to the Son as the greater reality, not merely an adjective modifying 'λόγος'.
Despite the lacuna, the context demands 'γεννητός' as the only semantically coherent restoration; the article 'τὸ' and the surrounding grammar require a nominalized adjective.

Another thing, or in the difference of the Son with respect to the created things he puts, saying that the Son indeed, but the things, slaves; and the Son indeed as Son sits with the Father at the right hand, but the things as slaves stand nearby and are sent out and serve; but these things having been written thus, the Son is not signified as begotten from these, O Arians, but rather another one indeed of the created things, but proper to the Father, being in his bosom; and for indeed the written thing here 'Having become' does not signify the Son as unbegotten, as you suppose; for if indeed simply he had said 'Having become' and had kept silent, there would have been an excuse for the Arians; but since he foretold 'Son', having demonstrated him throughout the whole passage to be another than the created things, he did not leave the word 'Having become' loose, but joined the more worthy to it; for he considered the word indifferent; knowing that on the one hand the one speaking 'Having become' of a genuine Son means the same as 'having been begotten' that he is greater, he says; for the generated thing indeed does not differ, even if someone says 'has come to be' or 'has been made'; but the created things, being creations, it is impossible to say they are begotten, unless perhaps after these things having partaken of the begotten Son, they are said to have been begotten and themselves; not a thing indeed through their own nature, but through the participation of the Son in the Spirit; and this again the divine Scripture knows, saying on the one hand of the created things 'All things through him came to be' and 'All things in wisdom he made'.

But concerning the sons born according to nature: 'Job had seven sons and three daughters,' and 'Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.' Therefore, if those born according to nature are one thing, and the substance of the Father alone is the proper offspring of the Son, the Arians' pretext concerning the one who became is refuted; for even if, ashamed in these matters, they force themselves to say again, the things stated comparatively are spoken comparatively, and therefore the things compared are of the same kind, so that they would be ashamed beforehand, as those who speak like Valentinus and Carpocrates, of whom one says the angels are consubstantial with Christ, the other says the angels of the world are creators; from them, perhaps, these also, having learned, compare the Word of God to the angels; but they would be ashamed imagining such things, when the hymn-singer says, 'Who shall be likened to the Lord among the sons of God?' and 'Who is like you among the gods, O Lord?' yet they would still hear, if they should learn, that among the consubstantial, likeness is commonly affirmed in comparison, and not among the heterogeneous; for no one would compare God to man, nor again man to the irrational, nor wood to stone, because of the dissimilarity of nature; but God is an incomparable thing, whereas man is compared to man, and wood to wood, and stone to stone; and no one could say, concerning these things, 'The stronger,' but rather 'the more' and 'the greater'; thus Joseph was more handsome than his brothers, and Rachel than Leah; and star is not stronger than star.
pass_b_english: Or again, in the distinction the Son bears toward creation, he declares: the Son is indeed the Son, but the created things are slaves. The Son, as Son, sits at the Father’s right hand; but the created things, as slaves, stand ready, are dispatched, and render service.

Given that these things are written in this way, the Son is not to be understood as begotten from them, O Arians; on the contrary, he is truly another—indeed, one of the created order in origin, yet properly belonging to the Father, dwelling in the Father’s bosom.

Moreover, the very wording here—‘Having become’—does not intend to mark the Son as unbegotten, as you mistakenly suppose. For if he had merely said ‘Having become’ and then fallen silent, that might have given you a pretext.

But since he had already affirmed the title ‘Son’ and demonstrated throughout this passage that the Son is essentially distinct from the created things, he did not leave the term ‘Having become’ isolated or insignificant; rather, he bound it to the greater reality.

For he regarded the word as indifferent in weight. Knowing full well that when one speaks of ‘Having become’ in reference to a genuine Son, the meaning is equivalent to ‘having been begotten’—and thus affirms the Son’s superiority—he declares it accordingly.
For the created thing, in its very nature, does not differ whether one says it ‘has come to be’ or ‘has been made.’

But the created things, as they are mere creations, cannot properly be called begotten—unless, that is, they have somehow received a share in the begotten Son, and thus, by participation, are spoken of as begotten themselves.
And this, too, the divine Scripture acknowledges: when speaking of the created things, it declares, ‘All things came to be through him,’ and ‘All things were made in wisdom.’

Indeed, when we look at sons born according to nature—like Job’s seven sons and three daughters, or Abraham, who was a hundred years old when Isaac was born to him—we see a clear distinction. Those born in the course of nature are one kind of thing, but the substance of the Father alone is the proper offspring of the Son. Therefore, the Arians’ pretext concerning the one who became is refuted. Even if, ashamed of this, they try again to speak comparatively, claiming that the things said are spoken only in comparison and that therefore the things compared must be of the same kind, they would still be ashamed beforehand, just like those who follow Valentinus and Carpocrates. For one of them says the angels are consubstantial with Christ, while the other says the angels of the world are creators. And perhaps these Arians, having learned from them, now compare the Word of God to the angels. Yet they would be ashamed to imagine such things, especially when the hymn-singer asks, 'Who shall be likened to the Lord among the sons of God?' and 'Who is like you among the gods, O Lord?' Still, if they were to learn, they would find that among consubstantial beings, likeness is commonly affirmed in comparison, but not among those of different kinds. For no one would compare God to man, or man to the irrational beasts, or wood to stone, because of the utter dissimilarity of their natures. Rather, God is an incomparable thing in Himself, while man is compared to man, wood to wood, and stone to stone. And concerning these things, no one would say 'the stronger,' but only 'the more' or 'the greater.' Thus Joseph was more handsome than his brothers, and Rachel than Leah; and one star is not stronger than another.

Therefore, the Son’s relation to the Father cannot be understood by comparing Him to creatures, even the highest, for such comparison assumes a likeness of nature that does not exist. The Arians err by treating the eternal Son as if He were merely the greatest among creatures, like the most handsome man.
